comments.author: @pxzallen
comments.text: Ardley Ab and Dry Island Ab have history of burning coal seams. Dry Island has lot of high temp clinker eroding out and deposited in the run off in small creeks. We find a lot of deeply buried burnt shale in southern Alberta. It is often mined and sold as "red shale" for landscaping. In Calgary during the 1979's most of the walking paths in parks were made of that red shale, 100's of kms.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Thanks for sharing that! The connection to Calgary’s old red shale paths is especially interesting, something people could walk over every day without thinking about its history. Have you explored those creek exposures yourself?

comments.author: @NorthOlbo
comments.text: I saw a lot of water analysis from rivers in northern Alberta with acid ph and lots of toxic metals, cadmium, mercury etc. the oil and forestry industries were blamed but there were no mills or energy activities within hundreds of km. The thick shale formation being cut through by streams was organic rich and oxidizing its carbon and deep sea metals. Exactly same process as Smoking Hills but not rich enough to actually burn. This explains a lot of bad water quality in areas nowhere near manmade sources. Great reason to support science and focus on things we can actually do something about.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Thanks for sharing that experience. Sulphide-rich shale can produce acidic, metal-rich drainage even without burning. Knowing the natural background is essential to working out what’s causing poor water quality. Which rivers were you looking at?

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: That’s an interesting approach. A dated offshore layer containing burnt material could show that burning had already happened by then. The tricky part is separating when the rock burned from when it slid into the sea, saltwater exposure alone wouldn’t give a straightforward date. I haven’t found a study testing that approach here, but it’s a thoughtful question.
